title: 1 Chronicles 29:10–19
context: David blesses the LORD before the assembly, confessing that greatness, power, glory, and the kingdom belong to God, and that riches and honor come from him. He asks who he and his people are that they could give so willingly, for all things come from God and they have given back of his own; they are strangers whose days are like a shadow. He prays that God would keep this desire in the hearts of his people and give Solomon a perfect heart; both traditions read the prayer as shared ground on grace, gratitude, and giving.

verses.text: Therefore David blessed the LORD before all the assembly; and David said, “You are blessed, LORD, the God of Israel our father, forever and ever.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You are blessed, LORD, the God of Israel our father, forever and ever.” Arminian readers note that David’s response to the offering is praise, not self-congratulation.

He turns attention from the gifts to the Giver.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the prayer beginning with God’s glory, which sets the tone for all that follows.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: worship responds to God’s goodness by blessing his name.

verses.text: Yours, LORD, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and on the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, LORD, and you are exalted as head above all.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Yours, LORD, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and on the earth is yours.” Arminian readers note the confession that all belongs to God.

“Yours is the kingdom, LORD.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a full confession of God’s sovereignty over all things.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the earthly kingdom David hands to Solomon belongs first to the LORD, who is “exalted as head above all.”

verses.text: Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all! In your hand is power and might! It is in your hand to make great, and to give strength to all!
verses.arminianNotes:
“Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all!” Arminian readers note that David attributes his wealth and honor to God.

“It is in your hand to make great, and to give strength to all!”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God as the source of every gift and every strength.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: human success and power are gifts from God, received with gratitude rather than pride (cf. Deut 8:17–18).

verses.text: Now therefore, our God, we thank you and praise your glorious name.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now therefore, our God, we thank you and praise your glorious name.” Arminian readers note that thanksgiving follows naturally from the confession of God’s greatness.

Praise is the fitting response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see gratitude as the heart of worship.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: thankfulness and praise belong together, and the “our” includes the whole assembly in the prayer.

verses.text: But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.” Arminian readers note that even the ability to give is God’s gift.

Giving returns to God what he first provided.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see grace behind the willing gift (cf. 1 Cor 4:7; Rom 11:35–36).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground on grace and giving: the people’s generosity is real and willing, and it flows from what God has given.

verses.text: For we are strangers before you and foreigners, as all our fathers were. Our days on the earth are as a shadow, and there is no remaining.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For we are strangers before you and foreigners, as all our fathers were. Our days on the earth are as a shadow.” Arminian readers note the humility of the confession, even at a moment of wealth.

The language recalls Leviticus 25:23 and Psalm 39:12.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the brevity of life set against God’s eternity.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: God’s people live as sojourners (cf. Heb 11:13), and wealth does not change that.

verses.text: LORD our God, all this store that we have prepared to build you a house for your holy name comes from your hand, and is all your own.
verses.arminianNotes:
“LORD our God, all this store that we have prepared to build you a house for your holy name comes from your hand, and is all your own.” Arminian readers note the repeated acknowledgment that everything belongs to God.

The offering is stewardship, not a gift that puts God in debt.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the same truth: the materials for God’s house come from God’s own hand.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: giving is an act of returning what God has entrusted.

verses.text: I know also, my God, that you try the heart and have pleasure in uprightness. As for me, in the uprightness of my heart I have willingly offered all these things. Now I have seen with joy your people, who are present here, offer willingly to you.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I know also, my God, that you try the heart and have pleasure in uprightness.” Arminian readers note that God values the motives of the giver.

David offers “in the uprightness of my heart” and rejoices in the people’s willing gifts.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s searching of the heart, as in 28:9 (cf. Ps 139:23).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: God delights in upright and willing hearts, and David’s joy is in the people’s generosity, not in his own.

verses.text: LORD, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Israel, our fathers, keep this desire forever in the thoughts of the heart of your people, and prepare their heart for you;
verses.arminianNotes:
David prays, “keep this desire forever in the thoughts of the heart of your people, and prepare their heart for you.” Arminian readers note that David prays for God’s continued help in sustaining the people’s devotion.

The prayer looks beyond the moment of giving.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see a prayer for God’s work in the hearts of his people (cf. Phil 2:13).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: willing hearts are sustained by God, and both pray for that sustaining work.

verses.text: and give to Solomon my son a perfect heart, to keep your commandments, your testimonies, and your statutes, and to do all these things, and to build the palace, for which I have made provision.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David asks, “give to Solomon my son a perfect heart, to keep your commandments, your testimonies, and your statutes.” Arminian readers note that David’s final request is for his son’s faithfulness.

The prayer echoes the charge in 28:9.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see David asking God to give what he has commanded.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the prayer for a perfect heart, and the later account of Solomon’s heart (1 Kings 11:4), call every reader to seek God’s help in faithfulness.
